One asked me to give him marks, I said I don't have any. Then he kicked me in the stomach. I looked around; I looked back. And then one Serbian soldier that was walking behind me shouted at the first one, Don't commit genocide, if we are going to kill him take a rifle in your hand and kill him like a soldier would. And one person in the column shouted, Give us first a drop of water to drink and then kill us. But nothing came of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I ask a question, please, sir. Do you know the name of this location where you were taken off the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name of the place of Branjevo which I didn't know at the time. I was not familiar with the area, but I heard it from the others that the name of the place was Branjevo, there were some barns there or stables. It was some kind of a farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witness, please continue. Can you describe where you were brought to by the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: We were brought to the place where the others had been killed. And they looked like they were arranged in neat order as if they were resting. And as we came to the place, we were walking through the lines of the bodies. And as we walked further, there were more and more of those aligned bodies. And as we came to the end of that, they told us, Align yourself up with the others and turn your backs towards us. Which is what we did. There were no orders given. Instead of fire, the order was, Lie down. But then we heard a burst of fire. I fell down immediately, and the others did as well. And then somebody asked, Are there any living? Is there anybody alive? And one said, I am alive. And the other also says, I am alive. Go on, kill me. I kept quiet. I didn't say anything. And then he shot a single bullet, actually he shot two bullets, and then they returned to fetch others, to fetch another column of people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: What did do you at this point, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: Well, I kept quiet. I was waiting to see what would happen. I was in two minds, whether I should raise my hand and be killed like the others, but I didn't, and they returned with another column of people. And they kept on bringing them and killing them and aligning them away from me. And they were killing them with bursts of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: How many columns were there as you lay -- did you hear being shot as you lay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: I believe six or seven more columns. And I don't know how many lines of bodies there were. I really did not feel like counting them. I just saw that there were many, that I was surrounded with bodies as far as my eye could see.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And how many people were in the columns? How many people were in your column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: On average anything between 20 and 27, I'd say. It all depended on how many got off the buses at a time. They would make two columns of one bus load of people. And that's how they killed. That's how they executed people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: What happened after the columns stopped coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: As the columns stopped coming, when everybody was killed, then they returned to the place where the buses were. They found shelter in the shade there, they rested. And then I tried to free my hands, but I couldn't. I tried to pull my hand out. I was lucky to be able to do so. And again I returned my hands into the ties while I was thinking. This gave me some time to think while my hands looked as if they were still tied behind my back. Because I knew that a patrol would come to inspect the bodies, and I knew that there was a chance that they would realise that I had released myself, that's why I placed my hands back in the ties. And they did indeed come, maybe twice or three times. They made rounds of the place. Once when they arrived, there were five of them. And then there was a shout, Look at him running. And there's another one. And then single bullets were fired. Four Serb soldiers went after them, went chasing them, and one stayed behind. When two of them returned, one asked the two of them what happened, and he said, Well, one got away, which means that they killed the other one.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witness, how did you escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: And then they were speaking to each other, We have committed genocide like the one in Jasenovac in 1941. That's what one of them said. And later when they left again, someone further down from me was whispering. I only turned my head a little and asked, Is there anyone alive? Come on, let's get out. And that's when I started untying myself. I took a look and saw two of them crawling into a thorn bush where I had meant to go. I also jumped to my feet. I walked on dead bodies. And I was also listening whether there would be a voice crying from somewhere, Look at him running, because if they see me, then I'm done for. Then so I also crawled into the thorn bush where the other two had gone. I looked behind myself and saw two more crawling behind me. They also came our way, and they had removed the traces so as not to be noticed. And everybody else was lying dead. But there weren't many bushes, maybe 100 or 150 square metres in all. And that's where we lay. Soldiers arrived again. They were walking among the dead, checking how things were standing, and we weren't far away from them. But then night fell, and they left. And we got out of the bushes on the opposite side, but on that side too, there were dead people lying around. Then we headed toward the forest where --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witness, may I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: How many people, how many bodies did you see, or how many bodies do you estimate there were that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: It's my estimate that there can't have been fewer than 1.000. Maybe between 1.000 and 1500, thereabouts. Of course I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And why do you estimate that amount?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: Because I saw how many dead bodies were lying in the field. The whole field was covered with dead bodies. And those who had surrendered in Potocari, they were both elderly people and children aged 14, but there were also 80-year-olds. Last year one man was buried who died at 84. I knew him personally. I said that their age was up to 80, but obviously there were also people over 80. They were all civilians, elderly people, children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Were any of your family members there that day?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, relevance?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I withdraw the question. Your Honour, if I may have one moment to confer with my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Witness, I'm not going to ask you about the further details of your escape and your survival, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MP-294
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam McKenna. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, based on the state of the record at present, coupled with the agreement that has been entered into, as well as the decision on adjudicated facts, it might be beneficial if we could have but five minutes so that we can confer with our client, after which point I think that things might move at a much quicker speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a short break and call us when you are ready. --- Break taken at 6.11 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I wish to thank the Chamber very much for that accommodation, as does Mr. Perisic. Based upon our discussion and the state of the record as it presently stands, we have no questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Witness, that brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for taking the time to come and testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused. You may stand down and travel well when you go back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I would like to thank you for having invited me here to tell the truth and to seek justice from you. And I wish to see Mladic as the next one to be tried here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Travel well home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That concludes our evidence for today. We have no further witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then, thank you. The matter will then stand adjourned to tomorrow, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no additional witnesses. The next witness we have scheduled is for the 28th of September, I'm informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, in that event the matter stands adjourned to the 28th of September, at 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of September, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.23 p.m.,
